fields.h1: Corrie ten Boom: Forgiveness in the Darkness
fields.meta_title: Corrie ten Boom: Forgiveness in the Darkness
fields.description: She survived a Nazi concentration camp and came out preaching forgiveness. The life of Corrie ten Boom — a witness that God’s love is deeper than any pit.
fields.body_html:
Corrie ten Boom survived one of the darkest places human cruelty has ever devised — a Nazi concentration camp — and came out preaching not revenge but forgiveness. A Dutch watchmaker’s daughter who hid Jewish people from the Nazis and paid for it with imprisonment and the loss of her family, she spent the rest of her long life travelling the world with a single message: that there is no darkness so deep that the light of God’s love cannot reach it, and no wound so grievous that his grace cannot heal it. Her life is one of the twentieth century’s most powerful witnesses to the reality of Christian forgiveness — costly, supernatural, and free. “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them” (Romans 12:14); Corrie learned to live those words in the very place designed to destroy them.

The hiding place

Corrie ten Boom was born in 1892 in Haarlem, in the Netherlands, into a devout family that ran a watchmaking shop. Her father, Casper, was a man of deep faith and deep love, and the ten Boom home was known for its hospitality and its love for the Jewish people. When the Nazis occupied Holland and began rounding up Jews, the ten Booms did not hesitate. They turned their home into a refuge, building a secret room — the “hiding place” — behind a false wall in Corrie’s bedroom, where Jewish neighbours and strangers could be concealed from the raids.

At great and knowing risk, the family sheltered and saved many lives. They understood that to love God meant to love their neighbour, and that the command to “rescue those who are being taken away to death” was not optional. For a time the secret held. But in 1944 the family was betrayed, and the Gestapo arrested them. The hidden Jews in the secret room were never found, but the ten Booms were taken away — and Corrie’s long descent into darkness began.

Into the concentration camp

Corrie’s beloved father died within days of the arrest. Corrie and her sister Betsie were eventually sent to Ravensbrück, a notorious women’s concentration camp in Germany, a place of starvation, disease, brutality, and death. There, amid unimaginable suffering, the two sisters clung to God and to a small, smuggled Bible, holding secret worship services that became a lifeline of hope to the desperate women around them. In the very heart of hell, they found that God was present.

Betsie, frail and gentle, grew ever more radiant in faith even as her body failed, insisting that God’s love was deeper than the deepest evil around them and that they must tell the world so when the war was over. She did not survive; Betsie died in Ravensbrück. Corrie was released shortly afterward through what she later learned was a clerical error — a mistake in the camp’s paperwork — just before the women her age were sent to their deaths. She walked out of Ravensbrück carrying her sister’s dying conviction that no pit is so deep that God’s love is not deeper still.

A message of forgiveness

Corrie emerged from the camp with a mission: to tell the world what she and Betsie had learned — that God’s love is stronger than the worst that human hatred can do, and that his grace makes even forgiveness of enemies possible. She began to travel and speak, and for more than thirty years she carried this message to dozens of countries, to millions of people, becoming one of the most beloved Christian witnesses of her century.

Her central theme was forgiveness, rooted in the words of Jesus: “For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you” (Matthew 6:14). She taught that we are to overcome evil not with more evil but with good (Romans 12:21), leaving vengeance to God — “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19) — and extending to others the same forgiveness we have received: “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). She had seen, in Ravensbrück, that hatred imprisons the hater, while forgiveness sets the forgiver free.

The hardest forgiveness of all

Corrie did not preach forgiveness as an untested theory. After the war, at a church in Germany where she had just spoken on God’s forgiveness, she was approached by a man she recognized with horror — one of the cruel guards from Ravensbrück, who had been among those who humiliated her and her dying sister. Now a Christian, he stretched out his hand and asked her to forgive him.

Corrie later described how she stood frozen, unable to forgive by her own strength, the memories of her sister’s suffering flooding back. She prayed silently for God to give her what she could not summon herself — and as she willed to obey and put out her hand, she felt God’s love flood through her, and forgiveness became real. It was, she said, not her own forgiveness but God’s, given through her. Her experience is one of the great modern illustrations of a profound truth: that God’s command to forgive comes with God’s power to obey, for “my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9), and even the crucified Christ prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34).

Light in the darkness

The great truth Corrie carried out of the camp, learned from her sister, was that there is no pit of human suffering or evil so deep that God is not deeper still. She had tested it in the worst place imaginable and found it true. Whatever a person had endured, however dark their memory or their present, she could look them in the eye and tell them, from her own experience, that God’s love reaches lower than the lowest depth, and that he is “a very present help in trouble” (Psalm 46:1).

This gave her words an authority that no comfortable preacher could match. She was not offering easy comfort from a safe distance; she had lost her father and her sister to the Nazis, had suffered in Ravensbrück, and still stood before the world declaring that God is good and his love unconquerable. In her, the promise came alive that in all these things “we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

Rebuilding lives after the war

Corrie’s forgiveness was not merely something she preached; it shaped what she built. After the war she opened a home in the Netherlands to care for those broken by the years of occupation and imprisonment — a place of rest and healing for camp survivors and others whose lives had been shattered. She had learned in Ravensbrück that bitterness only deepens the wound, and that those scarred by hatred needed a place to be loved back to life.

Remarkably, her ministry of reconciliation extended even to those on the other side. She came to see that the Dutch who had collaborated with the enemy also needed a way back, and that the gospel of forgiveness she preached must be offered to them too. This was forgiveness with its sleeves rolled up — not a sentiment but a labour, seeking the restoration even of former enemies. In it she lived out the hardest of Jesus’ commands: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44), and proved that the grace which had held her in the camp could also rebuild what hatred had destroyed.

Her enduring witness

Corrie ten Boom died in 1983, on her ninety-first birthday. She left behind a legacy far larger than her small frame — a testimony, retold in books and film and remembered around the world, that forgiveness is possible, that God is faithful in the darkest places, and that love is stronger than hate. She had every earthly reason for bitterness, and instead she gave her life to the ministry of reconciliation.

Her example still challenges and comforts. It challenges us, who nurse far smaller grievances, to forgive as we have been forgiven, remembering that “as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive” (Colossians 3:13). And it comforts us with the assurance, proved in a concentration camp, that no suffering can separate us from the love of God, and no darkness can outlast his light. Corrie ten Boom walked through the valley of the shadow and came out singing of grace — and her song still tells the world that God’s love is deeper than any pit. Few witnesses are harder to argue with, for she did not theorize about suffering from a comfortable study; she buried her family, endured the camp, and still declared God good. When such a woman tells us that forgiveness is possible and that God can be trusted in the dark, we are wise to listen — and to let her hard-won faith strengthen our own. Whatever pit you find yourself in today, her life stands as a quiet, unshakeable witness at its edge: God’s love is deeper still.
